chapter.title: When a station jams

cards.body:
On a real assembly line, when one station jams, a red light comes on above that station and the belt stops. Nobody tears down the factory. The foreman walks to the red light, reads the fault, and fixes that one station.

n8n works the same way. **Every run is logged, and the node that failed is marked red.** Your job is to walk to the light, not rebuild the line.
cards.simpler:
Think of a factory line where one machine gets stuck. A red light turns on above that machine and the belt stops. No one knocks the factory down. The foreman walks to the red light, reads the fault, and fixes that one machine.

n8n does the same. **Every run is logged, and the node that failed is marked red.** Your job is to walk to the light, not rebuild the line.

cards.prompt: Your Monday workflow posts a daily summary to Slack. Tuesday, nothing arrived and the office is quietly blaming you. What do you do first?

options.text: Delete the workflow and rebuild it from scratch, carefully this time
Open the Executions list and look at Tuesday's run
Add a second Slack node in case the first one is unreliable

whyNot.a: That's rebuilding the factory, not reading the red light: the fault is still unknown, so the same thing may break again.
whyNot.c: That's adding a station, not finding the jam: you don't yet know the Slack node is the one that failed.

cards.reteach: n8n keeps a record of every run, good and bad. Before changing anything, look at that record. It tells you which run failed and which single node stopped the belt.

cards.title: The shift log
cards.body:
Inside any workflow, next to the Editor tab, there is an *Executions* tab, a log of every time the workflow ran. Each row shows when it ran, how long it took, and a status: Succeeded or Error.

Click a failed row and the canvas opens showing that exact run. Nodes that worked have a green tick. **The node that failed is marked red.** Click it and the error message appears in its output panel.

Read the message slowly. It usually says what the outside app complained about, in its own words, and n8n often adds a plain hint beneath.
cards.simpler:
Open any workflow. Next to the Editor tab is an Executions tab. It lists every time the workflow ran. Each row shows the time, how long it took, and whether it succeeded or hit an error.

Click a failed row and the canvas shows that exact run. Nodes that worked have a green tick. **The node that failed is marked red.** Click it and the error message appears in its output panel.

Read the message slowly. It usually repeats what the outside app complained about, and n8n often adds a plain hint underneath.

cards.title: Thursday, 9:14
cards.body:
Priya's form-to-spreadsheet workflow ran fine for 3 weeks. Thursday at 9:14 the Executions list showed a red row. She clicked it: the Form Trigger, Edit Fields and IF nodes were green. The Google Sheets node was red.

The message said the sheet could not be found. A colleague had renamed the tab from Responses to Responses 2025 on Wednesday evening. Priya changed one field in one node, re-ran it, and watched the row land. Total repair time: shorter than the coffee she made first.
cards.simpler:
Priya's form-to-spreadsheet workflow had worked for 3 weeks. Thursday at 9:14 the Executions list showed a red row. She clicked it. The Form Trigger, Edit Fields and IF nodes were green. The Google Sheets node was red.

The message said the sheet could not be found. A colleague had renamed the tab from Responses to Responses 2025 on Wednesday evening. Priya changed one field in one node, re-ran it, and watched the row land. The fix took less time than making her coffee.

cards.prompt: A red run. Three nodes have green ticks, the fourth, a Slack node, is red. Where do you make a change?

options.text: The trigger node, because every run starts there
Only the Slack node, after reading its error message
All four nodes, to be safe

whyNot.a: That's the bell, not the jam: the green tick means the trigger did its job and passed items on.
whyNot.c: That's rebuilding, not repairing: three stations worked, so changing them can only add new problems.

cards.reteach: Green ticks mean those nodes finished and handed items on. The red node is where the belt stopped. Fix there, and only there, guided by what its message says.

cards.title: Re-run with the same part, then add a safety net
cards.body:
Fixing is easier when you can test with the exact item that broke. On a failed execution, n8n offers to load that run into the editor. Now the broken item sits in your canvas, so you can fix the red node and re-run it without waiting for another form to be submitted.

Two settings stop small faults becoming your problem. In a node's Settings tab, **Retry On Fail** tells n8n to try that node again, for example 3 times with a few seconds between, which handles a flaky connection.

In the workflow's own settings, *Error Workflow* names a second workflow that runs whenever this one fails. Make that one send you a message.
cards.simpler:
Fixing is easier when you can test with the exact item that broke. On a failed run, n8n offers to load that run into the editor. The broken item now sits in your canvas. You can fix the red node and re-run it without waiting for a new form to come in.

Two settings keep small faults from becoming your problem. In a node's Settings tab, **Retry On Fail** tells n8n to try that node again, say 3 times with a short pause between. That handles a shaky connection.

In the workflow's own settings, Error Workflow names a second workflow that runs whenever this one fails. Make that one send you a message.

cards.body:
Dev saw a red run, sighed, deleted the whole workflow and rebuilt it over lunch. It failed again at the same node, for the same reason: the sheet tab had been renamed, and no amount of rebuilding renames it back.

The tell is simple. If your hands are rebuilding before your eyes have read the error message, stop and go read it.
cards.simpler:
Dev saw a red run, sighed, deleted the whole workflow and rebuilt it over lunch. It failed again at the same node, for the same reason. The sheet tab had been renamed, and rebuilding does not rename it back.

The warning sign is easy to spot. If your hands are rebuilding before your eyes have read the error message, stop and go read it. It is like replacing a car because one tyre is flat.

cards.prompt: A friend texts: "My n8n thing broke, I'm starting over." What is the one line you send back?

options.text: Open Executions, click the red run, read the red node's message
Switch Active off and on, that clears the error
Turn on Retry On Fail for every node so it can never fail

whyNot.b: That's the on switch, not the log: toggling Active changes whether the workflow runs, not why it failed.
whyNot.c: That's the safety net, not the diagnosis: retries help with flaky connections, but a renamed sheet fails every one of the 3 tries.

cards.reteach: The Executions list is the shift log. A failed run shows exactly which node went red and keeps its error message. Reading that message is the whole first step, every time.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: When a workflow fails, open the Executions tab, click the red run, and the one node that broke is marked red with its error message waiting. **Fix that node, re-run with the same data, and add a retry or an error workflow** so next time it tells you itself.
cards.simpler: When a workflow fails, open the Executions tab and click the red run. The one node that broke is marked red, with its error message waiting for you. **Fix that node, re-run with the same data, and add a retry or an error workflow** so next time the workflow tells you itself. You fix the one stuck machine. You do not rebuild the whole factory line.

cards.body: Open the Executions tab on the workflow you built in chapter 3. Click the newest run. Open each node and look at the output it passed on. Then open the last node's Settings tab and find Retry On Fail.
cards.simpler: Open the Executions tab on the workflow you built in chapter 3. Click the newest run. Open each node one at a time and look at the output it passed on to the next one. Then open the last node's Settings tab and find Retry On Fail. You do not need to change anything yet. Just find where these things live so they feel familiar when something breaks.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now find which node failed, read why, and fix it without rebuilding the workflow.
